docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This datasheet documents my individual subsystem, the LiDAR subsystem, for OpenField, our RAS 304 team project. It collects the block diagram, component selections, bill of materials, schematic, and power budget for the LiDAR board.

docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text: OpenField is an open-source robot that sprays field lines, construction floor plans and temporary road markings using ordinary inverted spray-paint cans. It is built from commonly available parts with open firmware and hardware, as an affordable alternative to closed systems such as Dusty Robotics and HP SitePrint. The full team design is in our team report.

docs.title: My Contribution
docs.text: I am responsible for the LiDAR subsystem: a daughter board with its own PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano that reads a 360° time-of-flight LiDAR, reduces each scan to the obstacle and landmark data the robot needs to navigate, and sends it to the MASTER board over UART.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This block diagram shows how power and data flow through my LiDAR subsystem board for OpenField. The board reads a 360° LiDAR, processes each scan on its own PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano, and reports obstacle data to the team's MASTER board over the ribbon cable. It connects to the rest of the robot through Connector 1 in the team block diagram.

Figure 1: LiDAR subsystem block diagram. Click the image to enlarge it.

docs.title: Blocks
docs.text:
• Power source: A 3S lithium-ion pack (three 18650 cells in series, 9.0–12.6 V, 3000 mAh) plugs into the J1 barrel jack. On the bench, a 9 V adapter plugs into the same jack. See the Power Budget.
  • Protection and regulation: The input passes through F1, a 750 mA slow-blow fuse, to U2, an LM2940CT-5.0 low-dropout regulator with a heatsink. U2 makes the board's single +5 V rail.
  • Power levels: The +5 V rail powers the LiDAR (through jumper JP2) and the Curiosity Nano's VBUS pin (through Schottky diode D2 and jumper JP1). The Nano makes its own 3.3 V for the PIC and the debug LEDs. All grounds are shared, including ribbon pin 8.
  • Sensor: The Waveshare D500 time-of-flight LiDAR sends scan data on its TX line to RC7 (UART1 RX, 230400 baud). Its PWM speed input is left unconnected, so it uses its internal 10 Hz speed control.
  • Actuator: None on this board. The LiDAR's spinning motor is controlled inside the sensor.
  • User interface and debugging: Two debug LEDs (D3 red on RD0, D4 green on RD1) and a debounced pushbutton (SW1 on RA4).
  • Team connection: UART2 links the board to the MASTER board through Connector 1: RB0 (TX) goes to ribbon pin 2, and ribbon pin 1 comes in on RB1 (RX), at 115200 baud.

docs.title: Changes Since the First Version
docs.text:
• Added the power path (battery, barrel jack, fuse, and regulator), which the first version did not show.
  • Replaced the "TX/RX" LiDAR link with the D500's real interface: one TX data line, plus a PWM input that is left unconnected. The D500 has no RX line.
  • Added the debug LEDs and pushbutton, and labeled every connection with its pin, UART, and baud rate.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This page compares candidate parts for every major block in my LiDAR subsystem of OpenField (Team 1, Group 101), the open-source line-marking robot. The LiDAR subsystem is a daughter board with its own PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano. It reads a 360° ToF LiDAR, reduces the scan to the data the robot needs for navigation, and sends it to the MASTER board over UART (Connector 1, pins 1–2). See the Individual Block Diagram for how the blocks connect.

The major components on this board are:

  1. LiDAR Subsystem – Ranging sensor (ToF LiDAR)
  2. LiDAR Subsystem – +5 V voltage regulator (the "5V step-down" block)
  3. LiDAR Subsystem – Power source (the battery pack that feeds the regulator)

The PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano was selected for us and is not compared here (it does appear in the Power Budget).

docs.title: Design requirements that drive these choices
docs.text: Requirement Why it matters for the LiDAR board Works outdoors on grass, concrete and job sites OpenField marks sports fields, floor plans and road markings, so the sensor must tolerate bright ambient light and dust 360° obstacle and landmark detection out to several meters The robot needs to see walls, stakes, cones and people around it, not just straight ahead Interfaces directly with the PIC18F57Q43 UART at a rate the 8-bit PIC can parse, 3.3 V logic so no level shifting is needed Single +5 V supply from a linear regulator Course requirement; keeps the board to one rail Open-source friendly and commonly available Core to the OpenField pitch against Dusty Robotics and HP SitePrint Through-hole parts where practical RAS 304 boards are hand-soldered

docs.title: 1. LiDAR Subsystem – Ranging Sensor (ToF LiDAR)
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1.Slamtec RPLIDAR A1M8, 360° laser scanner\$99.95/eachRPLIDAR A1 at AdafruitA1M8 datasheet * Full 360° scan at 2–10 Hz with 8,000 samples/s and 1° angular resolution, enough to map the area around the robot* 12 m range covers a typical room or a section of a field* Very large user base and open-source SDK, so example parsing code is easy to find* 3.3 V TTL UART at 115200 baud, which the PIC can read directly * Laser triangulation ranging; the datasheet only rates it for outdoor use without direct sunlight, which conflicts with our sports-field and road-marking use cases* Highest current draw of the options: 300–350 mA for the core plus about 100 mA for the motor, with a 500–600 mA start-up surge* Large and heavy for our 3D-printed body (98.5 mm wide, 170 g)* Exposed spinning head collects dust and debris on a job site* Operating range only 0–45 °C Option 2.Waveshare D500 LiDAR Kit (LDRobot STL-19P, successor to the LD19)about \$50/eachD500 / LD19-class LiDAR on AmazonD500 wiki / protocol manual * About half the price of the RPLIDAR A1 (about \$50 vs. \$99.95), which keeps the team inside its budget* Direct time-of-flight (DTOF) ranging rated for 60 klux ambient light, much better suited to outdoor work than triangulation* Full 360° at 10 Hz, 5,000 measurements/s, 0.03–12 m range* Single +5 V supply runs both the sensor and its motor (290 mA working current), so only one rail is needed* Streams data on its own over a 3.3 V UART (230400 baud, 8N1); no start command is needed, which keeps PIC firmware simple* Built-in motor speed control, with an optional PWM input if we want to set the speed ourselves* Compact (38.6 × 38.6 × 33.5 mm), fits on top of the robot body* Supported by open-source ROS / Python drivers * Transmit-only interface; the PIC cannot request status or change settings except motor speed* 230400 baud stream uses about 85% of the UART's capacity, so the PIC must parse it with an interrupt or DMA, not polling* Data is in a vendor packet format with a CRC that we have to implement in C* The older LD19 version of this sensor is already discontinued, so we should buy a spare early* 60 klux still falls short of full summer sun (~100 klux), so a small sun hood may be needed Option 3 (custom).Sweeping scanner built from a Benewake TF-Luna single-point LiDAR on a TowerPro SG92R micro servo\$30.99 + \$5.95 = about \$37TF-Luna at Waveshare (wiki)SG92R servo at Adafruit * Lowest cost of the options (about \$37)* TF-Luna is rated for 70 klux ambient light, indoors and outdoors* Low sensor current (70 mA average, 150 mA peak)* Fully open design; we control the scan pattern and can point the sensor where the robot needs it (e.g. ahead only)* The PIC can drive the servo with a standard 50 Hz PWM output * Covers about 180°, not 360°; the robot is blind behind itself* Very slow scan: at 250 readings/s and 0.1 s/60° the servo gives roughly one 180° sweep every 0.3–0.6 s with 2–3° spacing between points* Range drops to 2.5 m on dark (10%) surfaces such as asphalt* Servo gears wear out under continuous sweeping, and servo current spikes add noise to the +5 V rail* We must design and print a mount and calibrate the servo angle, which adds mechanical work and error

Choice: Option 2: Waveshare D500 LiDAR Kit (LDRobot STL-19P)

Rationale: OpenField works outside, so sunlight tolerance is the deciding requirement. The RPLIDAR A1 uses triangulation and is only rated for use without direct sunlight. The D500 uses direct time-of-flight and is rated for 60 klux, while still giving the full 360° view that the custom servo scanner cannot. The D500 also draws less current than the A1 (290 mA vs. about 400 mA working and up to 600 mA at start-up), runs from the same +5 V rail as the Curiosity Nano, and outputs 3.3 V UART that connects straight to a PIC pin with no level shifter. Because it streams continuously without a start command, the PIC only needs a UART receive interrupt (or DMA) and a packet parser, which fits in the PIC18F57Q43's 8 KB of RAM (a 360-bin distance table is 720 bytes). It also comes with a published wiki and protocol manual, so there is real documentation to design against. Since the earlier LD19 has already been discontinued, the team should order a spare when we order the first unit.

docs.title: 2. LiDAR Subsystem – +5 V Voltage Regulator
docs.text:
The regulator takes the battery voltage down to the +5 V that powers the D500 and the Curiosity Nano's VBUS pin. The budgeted load is 502.5 mA including the 25% margin (see the Power Budget).

Solution Pros Cons Option 1.STMicroelectronics L7805CV, 5 V 1.5 A linear regulator (TO-220)\$0.75/each7805 at AdafruitL7805CV datasheet * Inexpensive and in stock almost everywhere, including the lab* 1.5 A rating gives three times the current we need* Through-hole TO-220 package is easy to solder and bolt to a heatsink* Low 6 mA quiescent current* Internal current limit and thermal shutdown * About 2 V dropout, so the input must stay above 7 V; it would not work if the team picks a 2S (7.4 V) pack* No reverse-battery protection; a backwards battery plug can destroy the regulator and the LiDAR* Like any linear regulator, it burns the extra voltage as heat (about 3.8 W at 12.6 V in), so it needs a heatsink Option 2.Texas Instruments LM2940CT-5.0/NOPB, 5 V 1 A low-dropout regulator (TO-220)\$1.94/eachLM2940CT-5.0 at DigiKeyLM2940 product page and datasheet * Low dropout (0.5 V typical, 1 V max at 1 A), so it works from any pack above 6 V: 2S or 3S LiPo, 9.6 V NiMH or 12 V lead-acid* Built-in reverse-battery protection, which protects the LiDAR from a backwards plug* 1 A rating is about twice the 502.5 mA we need* 26 V maximum input survives charger and motor-noise spikes* Same through-hole TO-220 footprint as the 7805 * Costs more than the 7805 (still under \$2)* Higher quiescent current (10–15 mA), which slightly shortens battery life* Needs a larger output capacitor (22 µF or more) for stability, per the datasheet* Still dissipates about 3.9 W at a full 3S pack and needs a heatsink Option 3 (custom).Discrete regulator: TIP31C NPN pass transistor driven by a 5.6 V zener (1N4734A) as an emitter followerabout \$1.50 in partsTIP31C at Wiltronics (\$0.88 AUD)TIP31C datasheet (ST) * Very inexpensive parts we already understand from class* TIP31C handles 3 A, so it has plenty of headroom* Good learning exercise and fully "open" with no IC behavior to trust * Poor regulation: output is the zener voltage minus VBE (about 4.9 V), which drifts with load and temperature and can fall below the Nano's 4.4 V VBUS minimum* No current limit or thermal shutdown, so a short can destroy the transistor or the LiDAR* No reverse-battery protection* More parts, more board space and more solder joints to fail* Zener bias current is wasted all the time

Choice: Option 2: Texas Instruments LM2940CT-5.0/NOPB

Rationale: The course requires a linear regulator, and this one was chosen before the battery was final, so it had to cover any likely pack. The LM2940's 1 V maximum dropout lets the same board run from a 2S LiPo, a 3S LiPo, a 9.6 V NiMH pack or a 12 V lead-acid battery, while the 7805 needs at least 7 V and rules out 2S packs. Its built-in reverse-battery protection matters on a robot whose battery is plugged and unplugged every session, since one backwards plug could destroy the LiDAR. Its 1 A rating covers the 502.5 mA budget with 497.5 mA left over. The custom transistor regulator was rejected because it cannot hold 5 V within the Curiosity Nano's VBUS limits and has no protection.

Thermal check: With a fully charged 3S pack (12.6 V) and the budgeted 502.5 mA load, the regulator dissipates about (12.6 V − 5 V) × 0.5025 A + 12.6 V × 0.015 A ≈ 4.0 W. To keep the junction below 125 °C at a 45 °C ambient (a robot running outside in Arizona), the total junction-to-air resistance must be under about 20 °C/W. A bare TO-220 is far above that, so the regulator gets a bolt-on TO-220 heatsink rated at about 15 °C/W or better, with thermal compound. If the team chooses a 2S pack, dissipation drops to about 1.8 W.

docs.title: 3. LiDAR Subsystem – Power Source
docs.text:
The power source feeds the LM2940 through the barrel jack J1. It has to keep the regulator's input above 6 V for the whole run, supply the 502.5 mA budget, and last at least 4 hours to meet the team's runtime requirement (PR-2).

Solution Pros Cons Option 1.9 V DC wall adapter, 1 A, 2.1 mm barrel plug * Steady 9 V with nothing to charge or replace* Lowest regulator heat of the three (about 2.0 W)* Plugs straight into J1 * Needs a wall outlet, so the robot cannot drive anywhere* Useful only for bench testing Option 2.3S Li-ion pack: three POWOBEST 3000 mAh 18650 cells in single-cell holders, wired in series, charged with HiLetgo TP4056 USB-C modules * 9.0 to 12.6 V over the whole discharge, always above the LM2940's 6 V minimum* 3000 mAh gives about 6.0 hours at 502.5 mA, well over the 4-hour requirement* Light and compact for a mobile robot* Cells are cheap, common, and replaceable one at a time* Charges from any USB-C supply with low-cost TP4056 modules * Most regulator heat at full charge (about 3.8 W), so the heatsink is required* Cells must be removed from the series holders to charge them one at a time* Lithium-ion cells need care: no crushing, over-charging, or over-discharging Option 3.8 × AA NiMH pack (9.6 V nominal, about 2000 mAh) * NiMH is a forgiving chemistry that is hard to damage* AA cells and chargers are easy to find * About 2000 mAh gives only about 4.0 hours, right at the requirement with no margin* Eight cells are heavier and bulkier than three 18650s* Voltage sags more under load

Choice: Option 2: 3S Li-ion pack (three POWOBEST 3000 mAh 18650 cells in series)

Rationale: The robot must drive on its own, which rules out the wall adapter except for bench testing. Between the battery options, the 3S Li-ion pack gives the longest runtime (about 6.0 hours vs. about 4.0 hours) at a lower weight, and its 9.0 to 12.6 V range always keeps the LM2940 in regulation. The cost is more heat in the regulator at full charge, which the TO-220 heatsink already handles (see the thermal check above). The 9 V adapter is kept as the bench supply, since it plugs into the same barrel jack.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This schematic is for my LiDAR subsystem board in OpenField (Team 1). The board uses a PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano to read a Waveshare D500 360° time-of-flight LiDAR on UART1 at 230400 baud. It processes the scan and sends the results to the team's MASTER board over UART2, through the 8-pin team ribbon cable shown in the team block diagram.

The parts match my Component Selection and Power Budget pages: a D500 LiDAR, an LM2940CT-5.0 linear regulator, and a 502.5 mA load on the +5 V rail (including the 25% safety margin).

Figure 1: LiDAR subsystem schematic, drawn in KiCad. Click the image to enlarge it.

docs.title: Schematic Sections
docs.text: Section What it does Key parts Power input, protection & 5 V regulation Accepts the board's own supply through a barrel jack: a 3S Li-ion battery pack (9.0–12.6 V) on the robot, or a 9 V DC adapter on the bench. The input passes through a removable 750 mA slow-blow fuse in an enclosed BLX-A holder. The fuse is sized for a 420 mA input load plus the LiDAR motor's start-up current. The 5 V rail is made by a through-hole linear LDO with the input and output capacitors its datasheet requires. A green LED shows the board is powered. Per the course project description, each board makes its own 5 V; only ground is shared over the ribbon. J1 PJ-063AH, F1 750 mA T in a BLX-A enclosed 5×20 mm holder, U2 LM2940CT-5.0 (TO-220, with heatsink), C1 100 µF/25 V, C2 0.47 µF/50 V, C3 22 µF/16 V, C4 0.1 µF, D1 Microcontroller PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano, drawn with my custom symbol (LK). The 5 V rail feeds the Nano's VBUS pin through a Schottky diode and a jumper, so a USB cable plugged into the Nano can't back-feed the board, and the board can't back-feed the USB port. VBUS and VTG each have a 0.1 µF bypass capacitor. Unused pins are marked no-connect. U1, D2 SS14, JP1, C5, C6 LiDAR interface 4-pin JST PH 2.0 mm through-hole header for the D500 (5 V, TX, PWM, GND). The LiDAR has its own power jumper and local capacitors (10 µF + 0.1 µF). Its TX line goes through a jumper to the PIC's UART1 RX. The PWM input is left floating (RC6 stays a high-impedance input) so the D500 uses its internal 10 Hz speed control, as the Waveshare D500 wiki specifies; the PIC can drive it through a 100 Ω resistor if needed. R3, a 10 k pull-down, is marked do-not-fit and is only for LD19-family sensors that need PWM grounded. J2 (custom D500 symbol, LK), JP2, JP3, C7, C8, R2, R3 (DNP), TP5, TP6 Team bus (ribbon cable) 2×4 IDC header to the MASTER board. Pin 1 is UART in (to RB1, the PIC's UART2 RX). Pin 2 is UART out (from RB0, UART2 TX). Pin 8 is GND. Pins 3–5 (digital) and 6–7 (analog) follow the course's team pinout and are unused on this board. Jumpers isolate both UART lines for debugging, and a 10 k pull-up keeps RX idle-high when the ribbon is unplugged. J3, JP4, JP5, R4, TP7, TP8 Debug LEDs & pushbutton Red debug LED (RD0) and green "LiDAR OK" status LED (RD1), each with a 330 Ω current-limiting resistor (about 4 mA). One pushbutton on RA4 with a 10 k pull-up and an RC hardware debounce (1 k + 1 µF, about 11 ms). D3, D4, R5, R6, SW1, R7, R8, C9 Expansion headers & test points Two 10-pin headers bring 16 spare GPIO pins (including ADC, I²C and SPI-capable pins) plus 3.3 V and GND out for future changes. Eight test points cover VIN, +5V, +3V3, GND, LIDAR_TX, LIDAR_PWM, UART_RX and UART_TX. J4, J5, TP1–TP8

docs.title: Design Notes
docs.text:
• Custom symbols (initials LK): the Curiosity Nano (U1), the D500 LiDAR connector (J2) and the voltage regulator (U2) are custom symbols in LK_CustomParts.kicad_sym. The Nano symbol groups its pins by port and puts the power pins on the top and bottom edges, which keeps the wiring clean.
  • Ratings: every resistor is 0805, 1/8 W, with at least 50% power margin (the worst case is 8 mW). Every capacitor's voltage rating is at least 25% above the rail it sits on: 25 V or 50 V on the 9–12 V rail, and 16 V or 50 V on the 5 V and 3.3 V rails.
  • Logic levels: the D500's UART runs at 3.3 V and the Nano's VTG is 3.3 V, so the LiDAR connects directly to the PIC with no level shifter.
  • Analog sensor / actuator requirement: per the instructor, this requirement applies to the whole system. It is met by the wheel subsystem (motor drivers and encoders) and the cliff-sensor subsystem, so the LiDAR board doesn't need its own.

docs.title: Breadboard Verification
docs.text:
Before finalizing the schematic, I breadboarded the core of the design: the D500 LiDAR, the Curiosity Nano and the two debug LEDs. The test checks the parts of the schematic that matter most: the LiDAR wiring and power, UART1 receiving at 230400 baud on RC7, the floating PWM pin, and the LEDs on RD0 and RD1.

Figure 2: The breadboard test running. The LiDAR spins, the green "LiDAR OK" LED (RD1) stays on while valid packets arrive, and the red debug LED (RD0) blinks as a heartbeat.

How it works: the PIC receives the D500's 47-byte packets on UART1 (RC7), checks each packet's CRC-8, and forwards the data stream to my laptop through the Curiosity Nano's USB serial port. A Python viewer on the laptop decodes the packets and plots a live 2D point cloud of the room.

Measurement Result LiDAR supply 5.00 V from a bench supply LiDAR running current 0.247 A (1.2 W), below the 290 mA used in the Power Budget Scan rate 9.9 Hz with the PWM pin left floating, confirming the D500's internal speed control (R3 stays DNP) Points per scan about 504 Packets received 143,674 good, 0 CRC errors

Figure 3: Live point cloud of the room drawn from the Nano's serial data, next to the bench supply reading.

Figure 4: Close-up of the breadboard: Curiosity Nano, debug LEDs with 330 Ω resistors, and the D500 LiDAR.

What I learned for the PCB:

  • Power path resistance matters. When the LiDAR's 5 V went through the breadboard rails, its motor start-up surge dropped the voltage below the D500's 4.5 V minimum and the LiDAR kept restarting. Wired directly to the supply, it started every time. On the PCB, the 5 V and GND traces to J2 will be wide, and C7/C8 sit right at the connector.
  • Check the cable pinout. My first attempt didn't work because the cable's wire order was reversed from what I expected. The J2 footprint pin order (1 TX, 2 PWM, 3 GND, 4 P5V) has to match the cable that will plug into it.
  • The firmware design works. Reading the LiDAR on UART1 and reporting over a second UART is the same structure the final board uses to send data to the MASTER board on UART2.

The test firmware (main.c, stage 6) and the point-cloud viewer (lidar_view.py) are available for download.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This power budget checks that the +5 V regulator selected on the Component Selection page can power everything on my LiDAR subsystem daughter board at the same time, with the required 25% safety margin. It follows the course power budget template; the filled-in spreadsheet is available under Resources.

The LiDAR board has one power rail (+5 V), made by an LM2940CT-5.0 regulator from a 3S Li-ion battery pack on the robot, or from a 9 V DC adapter on the bench. The Curiosity Nano makes its own 3.3 V target voltage (VTG) from its VBUS pin with its on-board MIC5353 regulator, so no separate 3.3 V regulator is needed and the +12 V and +3.3 V sections of the template are unused.

docs.title: A. Major Components
docs.text:
Component Part number Supply voltage range Qty. Max current (mA) Total current (mA) ToF LiDAR (Waveshare D500 / LDRobot STL-19P) STL-19P +4.5 to +5.5 V 1 290 290 PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano DM164150 +4.4 to +5.25 V (VBUS) 1 100 100

Current sources: 290 mA is the D500's rated working current from the Waveshare documentation. 100 mA for the Curiosity Nano is a conservative allowance covering the PIC18F57Q43 running at 64 MHz with UART, PWM and DMA active, plus the on-board nEDBG debugger chip, which is powered whenever the board is.

docs.title: B. +5 V Power Rail
docs.text:
Component Part number Supply voltage range Qty. Max current (mA) Total current (mA) ToF LiDAR (D500) STL-19P +4.5 to +5.5 V 1 290 290 PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano DM164150 +4.4 to +5.25 V 1 100 100 Indicator LEDs (D1 power, D3 debug, D4 "LiDAR OK") Green/red LEDs with 1 kΩ / 330 Ω resistors +3.3 to +5 V 3 4 12 Subtotal 402 Safety margin 25% Total current required on +5 V rail 502.5

The two debug LEDs run from the Nano's 3.3 V output, which the Nano makes from the +5 V rail, so their current is counted here. Each LED draws about (3.3 V − 2.0 V) / 330 Ω ≈ 4 mA. The power LED draws about 3 mA, rounded up to 4 mA.

docs.title: C. Regulator
docs.text:
Regulator Part number Input voltage range Qty. Max current (mA) Total current (mA) +5 V low-dropout linear regulator TI LM2940CT-5.0/NOPB +6 to +26 V 1 1000 1000 Total remaining current available on +5 V rail 497.5

The regulator selection table and rationale are on the Component Selection page.

Regulator heat: A linear regulator turns the extra input voltage into heat: P = (Vin − 5 V) × I.

Input Heat in the LM2940 at 502.5 mA 9 V (bench adapter, or an almost empty battery) (9 − 5) × 0.5025 ≈ 2.0 W 12.6 V (fully charged battery) (12.6 − 5) × 0.5025 ≈ 3.8 W

Both are too much for a bare TO-220 package, so U2 gets a TO-220 heatsink (about 15 °C/W or better).

docs.title: D. External Power Sources
docs.text:
The board has one power input, the barrel jack J1. On the robot, the battery pack plugs into J1. On the bench, a 9 V adapter plugs into J1 instead. Only one source is connected at a time.

Power source Part number Supply voltage range Output voltage Max current (mA) Total current (mA) Source 1 (robot): 3S Li-ion pack, three 18650 cells in series POWOBEST POWO18B 3000 mAh (×3) +9.0 to +12.6 V 11.1 V nominal 3000 3000 Rail connected: +5 V rail, through the LM2940CT-5.0 502.5 Total remaining current available on Source 1 2497.5 Source 2 (bench): 9 V DC wall adapter 2.1 mm barrel plug (fits J1, CUI PJ-063AH) 100 to 240 V AC 9 V DC 1000 1000 Rail connected: +5 V rail, through the LM2940CT-5.0 502.5 Total remaining current available on Source 2 497.5
  • Why 3S: Each 18650 cell is 3.7 V nominal (3.0 V empty, 4.2 V full). Three in series give 9.0 V to 12.6 V, which stays above the LM2940's 6 V minimum input for the whole discharge.
  • Battery current: The cell datasheet is not available, so the pack's maximum current is taken as 1C (3000 mA), a conservative continuous rating for an 18650 cell.
  • Input current: Because the LM2940 is a linear regulator, the current it takes from either source is about the same as the current it delivers on the +5 V rail.
  • Fuse: The 750 mA slow-blow fuse (F1) sits above the 502.5 mA load, leaving room for the LiDAR motor's start-up surge.
  • Charging: The cells are charged with TP4056 USB modules, one cell per module. To charge, the cells are taken out of the series holders, because single-cell chargers cannot safely charge cells while they are wired in series.

docs.title: E. Battery Life
docs.text:
Battery Part number Voltage range Capacity (mAh) Required by regulator (mA) Battery life 3S Li-ion pack POWOBEST POWO18B 3000 mAh (×3, in series) +9.0 to +12.6 V 3000 502.5 6.0 hours

Battery life = capacity ÷ current = 3000 mAh ÷ 502.5 mA ≈ 6.0 hours. (Cells in series add voltage, not capacity, so the pack is still 3000 mAh.)

Our team's product requirements call for at least 4 hours of runtime (PR-2). For 4 hours, this board needs at least 4 h × 502.5 mA ≈ 2,010 mAh, so the 3000 mAh pack meets the requirement with about 50% to spare.

docs.title: How the Power Budget Helped
docs.text:
• Regulator choice confirmed: The board needs 502.5 mA with a 25% safety margin. The LM2940CT-5.0 supplies 1000 mA, leaving 497.5 mA of headroom for the LiDAR motor's start-up surge.
  • Heatsink needed: The budget showed the regulator will burn 2.0 W to 3.8 W as heat, so I added a TO-220 heatsink to the design.
  • Fuse sized: The 750 mA slow-blow fuse sits above the normal 502.5 mA load but below the 1 A limits of both the adapter and the regulator.
  • Battery sized: The LiDAR board needs at least 2,010 mAh to meet the team's 4-hour runtime requirement. The 3000 mAh 3S pack gives about 6 hours.
  • Bench check: On the breadboard, the D500 drew 247 mA at 5.00 V, below the 290 mA used here, so the budget is conservative. (See Schematics.)
